title: Median
summary: For an odd sample the median is the middle order statistic. For an even sample this lesson averages the two middle values. A continuous median solves F(m)=0.5, and it need not equal the mean.
intuition:
The median is a middle, not a balance point. Sort the sample first. If the sample size $n=2k+1$ is odd, one order statistic sits in position $k+1$, and that value is the sample median. If $n=2k$ is even, two order statistics share the middle, in positions $k$ and $k+1$. Several conventions exist for that case. This lesson uses the average of those two middle values, and every even-sample answer below uses that convention.

For a continuous distribution the median is read from the cdf rather than from a list. A median $m$ satisfies $F(m)=0.5$. If $F$ is continuous and strictly increasing, there is exactly one such $m$. Probability 1/2 lies at or below $m$, and probability 1/2 lies at or above $m$. That is a statement about the distribution, not about the average of the values.

Mean and median part company when the distribution is skewed. A handful of large observations pulls the mean and leaves the middle order statistic where the bulk of the data sits. The density $f(x)=2x$ on $[0,1]$ does the same thing in reverse of the usual picture: its mean is $2/3$ and its median is $1/\sqrt{2}$, and $(2/3)^2=4/9<1/2$, so the mean is the smaller of the two. Reporting one of them as if it were the other is a different summary.

definitions.body: For a sample of size $n=2k+1$, sort it as $x_{(1)}\le\cdots\le x_{(n)}$. The median is the middle order statistic $x_{(k+1)}$.

For a sample of size $n=2k$, this lesson's convention sets the median equal to $\big(x_{(k)}+x_{(k+1)}\big)/2$, the average of the two middle order statistics. Other texts sometimes accept any point between them.
A number $m$ such that $F(m)=P(X\le m)=1/2$. If the cdf is continuous and strictly increasing, this equation has one solution.

formulas.name: Odd sample
formulas.note: Sort first. The middle position of the unsorted list is not the median.

formulas.name: Even sample, this lesson's convention
formulas.note: The average of the two central order statistics. Questions in this lesson use this convention.

formulas.name: Continuous median
formulas.note: For a continuous cdf. If $F$ is flat at height $1/2$, every point of that flat stretch is a median.

properties: At least half the observations are less than or equal to a sample median, and at least half are greater than or equal to it, up to the averaging step in the even convention.
Adding a constant $c$ to every observation adds $c$ to the median. Multiplying every observation by a positive constant $a$ multiplies the median by $a$.
The mean and the median of a symmetric distribution agree when both exist. Skew moves them apart.
For the density $f(x)=2x$ on $[0,1]$, the cdf is $F(x)=x^2$, the median is $1/\sqrt{2}$, and the mean is $2/3$. These are not equal.
A continuous distribution can have a whole interval of medians when the cdf stays equal to $1/2$ on that interval. The equation $F(m)=1/2$ then has more than one solution.

examples.title: An odd sample, sorted before it is read
examples.prompt: Find the median of the sample 12, 4, 9, 15, 7, 3, 11, and compare it with the sample mean.
steps: Sort the seven numbers: 3, 4, 7, 9, 11, 12, 15. The size $7=2\cdot 3+1$ is odd, so the median is the entry in position 4.
That entry is 9. The unsorted list has 15 in the middle slot, and 15 is not the median.
The sum is $12+4+9+15+7+3+11=61$, so the mean is $61/7$. Since $61/7\neq 9$, the mean and the median are different summaries of this sample.
examples.answer: The median is 9. The mean is $61/7$, which is not 9.

examples.title: An even sample, averaged
examples.prompt: Using the average-of-the-two-middle convention, find the median of 4, 10, 6, 18, and compare it with the mean.
steps: Sort the four numbers: 4, 6, 10, 18. The size is $4=2\cdot 2$, so the two middle order statistics are the 2nd and the 3rd, namely 6 and 10.
This lesson's convention averages them: $(6+10)/2=8$. Picking either 6 or 10 alone would be a different convention.
The mean is $(4+10+6+18)/4=38/4=19/2$. The mean $19/2$ and the median 8 are not equal.
examples.answer: The median is 8, and the mean is $19/2$.

traps: Reading the middle entry of the unsorted list. In 12, 4, 9, 15, 7, 3, 11 the centre of the raw list is 15, and the median is 9.
For an even sample, reporting one of the two middle order statistics instead of their average. Under this lesson's convention, 6 and 10 give 8, not 6 and not 10.
Equating the mean and the median for a skewed sample. The sample 2, 2, 2, 2, 14 has median 2 and mean $22/5$.
Solving $f(m)=1/2$ instead of $F(m)=1/2$. The median condition is on the cdf. For $f(x)=2x$ on $[0,1]$ the density equals $1/2$ at $x=1/4$, while the median is $1/\sqrt{2}$.
python:
odd = sorted([12, 4, 9, 15, 7, 3, 11])
assert odd[len(odd) // 2] == 9
assert sum([12, 4, 9, 15, 7, 3, 11]) == 61
even = sorted([4, 10, 6, 18])
k = len(even) // 2
assert (even[k - 1] + even[k]) / 2 == 8
skew = sorted([2, 2, 2, 2, 14])
assert skew[2] == 2 and sum(skew) == 22
pair = sorted([1, 2, 3, 8])
assert (pair[1] + pair[2]) / 2 == 2.5
assert (2 / 3) ** 2 < 0.5  # mean squared versus median squared
print(9, 8, 2.5)

questions.stem: The median of the sample 9, 1, 4, 1, 7 is
questions.solution:
The answer is **A**, $4$.

Sort first: 1, 1, 4, 7, 9. The size 5 is odd, so the median is the third order statistic, which is 4. Option D is the mean $(9+1+4+1+7)/5=22/5$, a different summary. Option B is the smallest value, which is tied but is not the middle.

questions.stem: Under the convention that an even sample median is the average of the two middle order statistics, the median of 3, 9, 5, 15 is
questions.solution:
The answer is **A**, $7$.

The sorted sample is 3, 5, 9, 15. The two middle values are 5 and 9, and their average is 7. Options B and C are those middle values taken separately, which this convention does not do. Option D is the mean $(3+9+5+15)/4=8$.

questions.stem: Which of the following are true?
options: If a continuous cdf $F$ is strictly increasing, the median is the unique solution of $F(m)=1/2$.
For a sample of odd size, the median is the middle value after the sample is sorted.
Under this lesson's convention, the median of an even sample is the average of the two middle order statistics.
The mean and the median are equal for every data set.
questions.solution:
The correct options are **A, B, and C**.

A is the continuous definition when the cdf cannot pause at height $1/2$. B is the odd-sample rule, and the sort is required. C is the even-sample convention used throughout this lesson. D fails for 2, 2, 2, 2, 14, whose median is 2 and whose mean is $22/5$.

questions.stem: Enter the median of the sample 6, 2, 9, 4, 11.
questions.solution:
The answer is **6**.

Sort the five numbers: 2, 4, 6, 9, 11. The size is odd, so the median is the third order statistic, which is 6. The mean is $(6+2+9+4+11)/5=32/5$, which is not the median.

questions.stem: Under the convention that an even sample median is the average of the two middle order statistics, the sample 1, 2, 3, 8 has median $m$. Enter $2m$.
questions.solution:
The answer is **5**.

The sorted sample is 1, 2, 3, 8. The two middle order statistics are 2 and 3, so $m=(2+3)/2=5/2$ and $2m=5$. Reporting either middle value alone would not match this convention.
